messages.content: Suppose a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) converge pointwise to f(x) on [0, 1]. Does it follow that the B_n converge uniformly? Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 20% of the total words in your response.

message.content: No. Counterexample: B_n(x) = x^n. Pointwise limit f: f(x) = 0 for x ∈ [0,1), f(1) = 1. Discontinuous. Sup |B_n − f| = 1 always. Non-uniform. Polynomials can yield discontinuous pointwise limits on compact intervals; continuity of f is necessary for uniform convergence.

A better counterexample: Consider B_n(x) = (x/n)^n on [0,1]. For x ∈ [0,1], as n→∞, (x/n)^n → 0. So f(x) = 0 for all x ∈ [0,1]. But sup_{x∈[0,1]} |B_n(x) - 0| = max_{x∈[0,1]} (x/n)^n = (1/n)^n → 0. Wait, that DOES converge uniformly.

Not uniform convergence since sup |x^n - f(x)| = sup over x near 1 of |x^n - 0| = 1^n - 0 = ... wait, at x=1, f(1)=1 so |1^n - 1| = 0. At x ∈ [0,1), f(x)=0, so |x^n - 0| = x^n. The sup of x^n over [0,1) is approaching 1 but never reaching it. So sup |B_n(x) - f(x)| = sup_{x∈[0,1)} x^n = 1 (supremum, not maximum). So the convergence is not uniform.

This is a valid counterexample. The polynomials B_n(x) = x^n converge pointwise to f(x) = 1_{x=1} on [0,1], but not uniformly.
